concept.name: Credit factor
concept.definition: One of the two bond-market factors in Fama and French (1993), capturing default risk: DEF is the difference between the return on long-term corporate bonds and the return on long-term government bonds, proxying the compensation for bearing corporate default risk.
concept.intuition: Corporate bonds pay more than Treasuries because they can default; DEF measures, each period, how much that credit exposure actually earned or lost.
concept.mechanics: Constructed as the return spread of long-term corporate bonds over long-term government bonds; in factor regressions for corporate bond portfolios, DEF typically carries the majority of explanatory power because long-only credit portfolios share common market exposure to the default premium.
concept.formula: DEF_t = R_LTC,t - R_LTG,t, where R_LTC is the return on long-term corporate bonds and R_LTG the return on long-term government bonds.
concept.failure_modes: DEF bundles duration-matched credit spread changes with actual default losses and flight-to-quality episodes; it spikes negatively in crises (credit widening) and cannot distinguish compensation for expected defaults from compensation for default-risk volatility.
concept.misconceptions: DEF is not the credit spread itself: it is the realized excess return of corporate over government bonds, which is negative whenever spreads widen enough to offset the yield advantage.
concept.example: If long-term corporate bonds return -0.5% in a month while long-term Treasuries return +1.0% amid a flight to quality, DEF realizes -1.5%, hitting credit-heavy portfolios.

citations.source: Bektic, Wenzler, Wegener, Schiereck, and Spielmann, Extending Fama-French Factors to Corporate Bond Markets (working paper, describing the Fama-French 1993 TERM and DEF factors)
citations.section: Section 4.1 (DEF as corporate bond market excess returns / default premium)
